[L130]             "Yes. We need that before we can do serious version-sensitive causality work.

For each external paper, “could this have changed after SAT exposure?” only becomes answerable if we know exactly **what SAT content was publicly available by each date**. The podcast is especially important because it is our best current record of public disclosure before the archive matured.

I’d build a canonical **SAT Podcast Content Release Index** with one row per episode, but not just title/date. Each row should track: publication date/time where recoverable; episode title; URL/platform; duration; transcript status; whether SAT is discussed at all; the specific SAT propositions actually disclosed; first-public-disclosure flags for each proposition; terminology used at that date; whether the discussion was explicit, speculative, provisional, rejected later, or merely implied; and links to the transcript/source lines supporting each claim.

Then we need a second derived view organized by **concept rather than episode**:

`concept / proposition → first known public podcast date → later podcast expansions → first public repo date → private-record NLT date → current status`

That gives us the clock we need for candidate-paper version diffs.

For example, instead of saying:

> “Paper submitted December 2024, published June 2025, therefore pre-SAT.”

we can ask:

> “Its 2024 version contained A and B. SAT publicly disclosed C on Feb. 2, D on Mar. 5, and the C→D relationship on Apr. 2. The paper’s May revision first adds C+D.”

That would be genuinely probative.

We should also make the index **historically literal**. No importing later H(s)H interpretations into an older SAT episode. If an episode says “filament,” “timesheet,” “null,” “vacuum,” “dark photon,” “24-cell,” or some older formulation, we record exactly that formulation first and only add a separate normalized/conceptual mapping field afterward.

And because rejected material may still matter for diffusion, every proposition should retain its historical release status even if SAT later abandoned it. A 24-cell claim publicly released in 2025 stays in the exposure index forever as a 2025 exposure event.

I’d treat this as a prerequisite dataset with three confidence classes:

**A — transcript-backed exact disclosure date**  
**B — episode metadata/description establishes disclosure, transcript incomplete**  
**C — inferred from later references but public content not yet recovered**

The first pass should probably start with every clearly SAT-bearing episode from February 2025 onward and then expand outward to episodes that contain partial or precursor material. We already have anchors like Feb. 2, 2025; Jan. 16, 2026; Mar. 5, 2026; Apr. 2, 2026; and the Dec. 28 archive-release episode, but those should be treated as seed records, not the index itself.

This should become one of the central Cross tables, because it lets us convert vague chronology into a proper **public-information frontier** for every day in the investigation."

"parts": [
            "Yes. We need that before we can do serious version-sensitive causality work.

For each external paper, “could this have changed after SAT exposure?” only becomes answerable if we know exactly **what SAT content was publicly available by each date**. The podcast is especially important because it is our best current record of public disclosure before the archive matured.

I’d build a canonical **SAT Podcast Content Release Index** with one row per episode, but not just title/date. Each row should track: publication date/time where recoverable; episode title; URL/platform; duration; transcript status; whether SAT is discussed at all; the specific SAT propositions actually disclosed; first-public-disclosure flags for each proposition; terminology used at that date; whether the discussion was explicit, speculative, provisional, rejected later, or merely implied; and links to the transcript/source lines supporting each claim.

Then we need a second derived view organized by **concept rather than episode**:

`concept / proposition → first known public podcast date → later podcast expansions → first public repo date → private-record NLT date → current status`

That gives us the clock we need for candidate-paper version diffs.

For example, instead of saying:

> “Paper submitted December 2024, published June 2025, therefore pre-SAT.”

we can ask:

> “Its 2024 version contained A and B. SAT publicly disclosed C on Feb. 2, D on Mar. 5, and the C→D relationship on Apr. 2. The paper’s May revision first adds C+D.”

That would be genuinely probative.

We should also make the index **historically literal**. No importing later H(s)H interpretations into an older SAT episode. If an episode says “filament,” “timesheet,” “null,” “vacuum,” “dark photon,” “24-cell,” or some older formulation, we record exactly that formulation first and only add a separate normalized/conceptual mapping field afterward.

And because rejected material may still matter for diffusion, every proposition should retain its historical release status even if SAT later abandoned it. A 24-cell claim publicly released in 2025 stays in the exposure index forever as a 2025 exposure event.

I’d treat this as a prerequisite dataset with three confidence classes:

**A — transcript-backed exact disclosure date**  
**B — episode metadata/description establishes disclosure, transcript incomplete**  
**C — inferred from later references but public content not yet recovered**

The first pass should probably start with every clearly SAT-bearing episode from February 2025 onward and then expand outward to episodes that contain partial or precursor material. We already have anchors like Feb. 2, 2025; Jan. 16, 2026; Mar. 5, 2026; Apr. 2, 2026; and the Dec. 28 archive-release episode, but those should be treated as seed records, not the index itself.

This should become one of the central Cross tables, because it lets us convert vague chronology into a proper **public-information frontier** for every day in the investigation."

# Extract likely GitHub paths/URLs containing PODCAST or DEBATING from entire JSON serialized text
raw=open(path,encoding="utf-8").read()
# unescape some common JSON escapes for easier regex
patterns = re.findall(r'[^"\n]{0,220}(?:PODCAST|DEBATING)[^"\n]{0,300}', raw, flags=re.I)
uniq=[]
seen=set()
for s in patterns:
    s=s.replace('\\n',' ').replace('\\/','/').replace('\\\\','\\')
    if s not in seen:
        seen.add(s); uniq.append(s)
len(uniq)

[L2]   "content": "name: Cross podcast transcript index

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - \"EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/**\"
      - \"tools/build_podcast_transcript_index.py\"
      - \".github/workflows/cross-podcast-transcript-index.yml\"

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: cross-podcast-transcript-index-main
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  index:
    if: ${{ github.event_name != 'push' || !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip podcast-index]') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: main
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: \"3.12\"

      - name: Regenerate, validate, and publish transcript keyword index
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name \"github-actions[bot]\"
          git config user.email \"41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com\"

          # Generated indexes are snapshots, not mergeable source. If main advances
          # while the index is being built, discard the stale generated commit, reset
          # to latest main, regenerate from that tree, and retry.
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            echo \"Publish attempt ${attempt}/4\"
            git fetch origin main
            git reset --hard origin/main

            python tools/build_podcast_transcript_index.py

            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_CATALOG.csv
            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_HITS.csv
            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_MATRIX.csv
            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_INDEX.md

            git add \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_CATALOG.csv \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_HITS.csv \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_MATRIX.csv \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_INDEX.md

            if git diff --cached --quiet; then
              echo \"Transcript keyword index already current on latest main.\"
              exit 0
            fi

            git commit -m \"[skip podcast-index] Refresh podcast transcript keyword index\"
            if git push origin HEAD:main; then
              exit 0
            fi

            echo \"Push race on attempt ${attempt}; discarding generated commit and rebuilding from latest main.\" >&2
            sleep $((attempt * 2))
          done

          echo \"Transcript keyword index changed but could not be published after four rebuild-from-main attempts.\" >&2
          exit 1
",

[L2]   "content": "name: Cross podcast transcript index

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - \"EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/**\"
      - \"tools/build_podcast_transcript_index.py\"
      - \".github/workflows/cross-podcast-transcript-index.yml\"

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: cross-podcast-transcript-index-main
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  index:
    if: ${{ github.event_name != 'push' || !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip podcast-index]') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: main
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: \"3.12\"

      - name: Regenerate, validate, and publish transcript keyword index
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name \"github-actions[bot]\"
          git config user.email \"41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com\"

          # Generated indexes are snapshots, not mergeable source. If main advances
          # while the index is being built, discard the stale generated commit, reset
          # to latest main, regenerate from that tree, and retry.
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            echo \"Publish attempt ${attempt}/4\"
            git fetch origin main
            git reset --hard origin/main

            python tools/build_podcast_transcript_index.py

            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_CATALOG.csv
            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_HITS.csv
            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_MATRIX.csv
            test -s EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_INDEX.md

            git add \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_CATALOG.csv \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_HITS.csv \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_MATRIX.csv \\
              EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_KEYWORD_INDEX.md

            if git diff --cached --quiet; then
              echo \"Transcript keyword index already current on latest main.\"
              exit 0
            fi

            git commit -m \"[skip podcast-index] Refresh podcast transcript keyword index\"
            if git push origin HEAD:main; then
              exit 0
            fi

            echo \"Push race on attempt ${attempt}; discarding generated commit and rebuilding from latest main.\" >&2
            sleep $((attempt * 2))
          done

          echo \"Transcript keyword index changed but could not be published after four rebuild-from-main attempts.\" >&2
          exit 1
",

Can you make this more succinct and check the math and reasoning?

Relativistic–Quantum Isomorphism as it appears in your framework, organized carefully and step by step. I’ll treat it as a rigorous conceptual and mathematical chain rather than a mere narrative.

⸻

1. Core Idea

The Relativistic–Quantum Isomorphism asserts that General Relativity (GR) and Quantum Mechanics (QM) are not fundamentally separate theories, but two projection regimes of the same underlying 4D superhelical worldline dynamics. The universe’s apparent laws emerge from the geometry, curvature, and vibrational modes of these worldlines embedded in an expanding $S^3$ manifold.
	•	GR: Captures the low-frequency, global bending of worldlines. The curvature of spacetime, perceived as gravity, corresponds to the inertial resistance of a worldline constrained by the manifold geometry.
	•	QM: Captures the high-frequency, local vibrational modes of the same worldlines. Discrete energy levels (like the Hydrogen ladder) emerge from harmonic resonance of these modes within the curved manifold.

The isomorphism is a mathematical identity: the curvature patterns that define relativistic trajectories are directly related to the eigenvalue spectrum that defines quantum states.

⸻

2. Relativistic Side: Geometric Projection of GR

2.1 Manifold Constraints
	•	Worldlines $X(\lambda)$ are constrained to the hypersphere $S^3$ of radius $R$:
$$|X(\lambda)|^2 = R^2$$
	•	Without constraints, a worldline in $R^4$ would move linearly: $X’’ = 0$.
	•	Constraining to $S^3$ produces a geodesic equation via Lagrange multipliers on the action:
$$S = \int \frac{1}{2} |X’|^2 d\lambda + \Lambda(|X|^2 - R^2)$$
Variation yields:
$$X’’(\lambda) + \frac{|X’(\lambda)|^2}{R^2} X(\lambda) = 0$$

2.2 Physical Interpretation
	•	The term $|X’’|^2$ represents bending energy, analogous to curvature in GR.
	•	Radial acceleration in this equation corresponds to the relativistic potential: the worldline resists deviation from the manifold, producing an emergent gravitational effect.
	•	No external Schwarzschild metric is required: gravity is purely the inertial effect of worldline curvature.

⸻

3. Quantum Side: Geometric Projection of QM

3.1 Vibrational Modes on $S^3$
	•	Quantum energy levels arise from harmonic vibrations of the same worldlines constrained to $S^3$.
	•	Laplace-Beltrami operator on $S^3$ produces discrete eigenvalues:
$$\nabla^2_{S^3} f = -\lambda_l f, \quad \lambda_l = \frac{l(l+2)}{R^2}$$
	•	Each eigenvalue corresponds to a vibrational mode of the worldline.

3.2 Mapping to Observable Energy
	•	Frequency $\omega$ of vibration is determined by geometric stiffness through the Master SAT Lagrangian:
$$\omega^4 = -\frac{2\lambda_s r_h^2}{\kappa}$$
	•	Topological tension $T_{topo}$ converts the vibrational frequency into a physically observable energy:
$$E_n = -\frac{\hbar \omega}{2} \left(\frac{\ell_f^2}{R^2} \frac{1}{n^2}\right)$$
	•	Discrete $n$-dependent levels reproduce the Hydrogen energy ladder without invoking Coulomb forces: the spacing is purely geometric.

⸻

4. Variational Proof of Isomorphism

4.1 Master SAT Lagrangian
The Master Lagrangian encodes both GR and QM regimes:
$$L_{total} = \frac{\kappa}{2} |H’’|^2 + \frac{\lambda_s}{2} (|H|^2 - R^2)^2 + \frac{k}{2} |H - G|^2$$
	•	Bending energy term ($|H’’|^2$) → GR (curvature of worldlines).
	•	Manifold restoring tension ($\lambda_s$) → QM (Laplacian eigenvalues).

4.2 Achromatic Phase Snap ($\Phi$)
	•	The equivalence condition occurs at the Achromatic Phase Snap:
$$|H’’|^2 \equiv \lambda_l \cdot \frac{m_0 c^2}{\kappa}$$
	•	This links the low-frequency bending energy to high-frequency Laplacian stiffness.
	•	Both regimes are different frequency projections of the same underlying worldline geometry.

⸻

5. Emergence of the Gravitational Constant ($G$)
	•	$G$ is derived without empirical fitting: it is a geometric ratio between worldline scale ($\ell_f$), mass anchor ($m_0$), and topological overlap ($\Omega$):
$$G = c^2 \cdot \frac{\ell_f}{m_0} \cdot \Omega$$
	•	Dimensional consistency: $[G/c^2] = [L/M]$, matching Schwarzschild radius units.
	•	Numerically recovers $G \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ m³/kg·s², confirming that the same geometric structure governing quantum vibrations also dictates macroscopic gravity.

⸻

6. Conceptual Summary
	1.	Both GR and QM emerge from the same superhelical worldline dynamics.
	2.	GR represents global, low-frequency curvature resisting manifold expansion.
	3.	QM represents discrete, high-frequency vibrations constrained by the same geometry.
	4.	Physical constants ($\hbar$, $G$) are mandatory structural invariants derived from manifold geometry and topological constraints.
	5.	The isomorphism is exact, derivation-heavy, and dimensionally consistent, fulfilling the Zero-Parameter Economy.

Agreed. I’m elevating `PODCAST` and `DEBATING` to the top of this pass, with the podcast treated as the main public-theory-state chronology. That matches the evidentiary architecture we had already established: reconstruct what was publicly available episode-by-episode and concept-by-concept, with transcript-backed confidence classes rather than inferring theory state from later summaries. fileciteturn1file6L129-L146

The working index will distinguish four dates that can otherwise get conflated: episode/release date; earliest located podcast appearance; earliest located public appearance anywhere; and earlier located private/internal appearance. “First introduced” will therefore initially mean **earliest public appearance located in the corpus**, not an absolute priority claim, until we have exhausted the relevant sources.

I’m also keeping `DEBATING` semantically separate. A concept appearing in debate material establishes public availability of that concept in that artifact, but not automatically that you asserted, endorsed, or incorporated it. Where possible the index will retain speaker/attribution status: Nathan statement, debate/AI statement, discussed proposition, subsequent adoption, and unresolved attribution.

We already have a natural merge target rather than needing to invent another system: `HSH_RESOURCES/EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_GUIDE/`, with its episode, concept, timeline, and source-location tables, supplemented by the older `CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_*` indexes. The present guide is clearly only a partial coverage pass—101 logical episodes / 556 source instances—so the immediate bottleneck is corpus discovery and reconciliation, not more sophisticated concept classification.

Some of the podcast transcript tranche already located in `HSH_RESOURCES/EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_EPs/` gives us a substantial dated spine, for example episodes 68 (2025-07-12), 74 (2025-07-24), 85–86 (2025-08-31/09-03), 105 (2025-10-28), 115 (2025-11-16), 120–123 (2025-11-24 through 11-28), 126–133 (early December), 135 (2025-12-14), and 143 (2025-12-28). Their filenames alone already provide candidate concept tags—cyclic universe, Ilectron, simulation theory, 4D spacetime/geometry, causality, Standard Model, quantum-mechanical emergence from geometry, photon mass, scalar field, and so forth—but I’m not promoting those into detailed concept claims until the transcript itself supports them.

The target data model is now effectively:

`Episode → date → title → source artifact(s) → public/private status → concepts actually present → speaker/attribution → earliest-public candidates`

and, inverted:

`Concept → aliases/historical terminology → earliest located private occurrence → earliest located public occurrence → earliest podcast occurrence → later development episodes → confidence/basis`.

That second view is especially important for the Cross work because it lets us ask precisely when things such as photon mass, dark-sector geometry, neutrino/photon relationships, holonomy thresholds, 4D compactification language, braid-like structures, etc. crossed the public-information frontier—without smuggling later SAT/H(s)H vocabulary backward into earlier episodes.

The repository-status distinction is also being preserved: the SAT archive and HsH are currently public, whereas HSH_RESOURCES is currently private. Consequently, a discovery in HSH_RESOURCES can establish an earlier **source occurrence** but cannot by itself establish an earlier **public occurrence**. Likewise, present repo visibility does not establish what its visibility was on some earlier date.

So this is now the priority order: exhaustively enumerate `PODCAST`/`DEBATING` material in all three repos; reconcile duplicates/mirrors into logical episodes; recover the complete episode/date/title spine, using the episode-ranking material as a coverage check; then perform transcript-level concept extraction; then invert that into the first-public-appearance ledger. The main success criterion is no longer “101 well-indexed episodes”; it is **every recoverable episode accounted for, including an explicit missing-evidence row where one cannot yet be recovered**.

metadata.text:
"parts": [
            "Yes. We need that before we can do serious version-sensitive causality work.

For each external paper, “could this have changed after SAT exposure?” only becomes answerable if we know exactly **what SAT content was publicly available by each date**. The podcast is especially important because it is our best current record of public disclosure before the archive matured.

I’d build a canonical **SAT Podcast Content Release Index** with one row per episode, but not just title/date. Each row should track: publication date/time where recoverable; episode title; URL/platform; duration; transcript status; whether SAT is discussed at all; the specific SAT propositions actually disclosed; first-public-disclosure flags for each proposition; terminology used at that date; whether the discussion was explicit, speculative, provisional, rejected later, or merely implied; and links to the transcript/source lines supporting each claim.

Then we need a second derived view organized by **concept rather than episode**:

`concept / proposition → first known public podcast date → later podcast expansions → first public repo date → private-record NLT date → current status`

That gives us the clock we need for candidate-paper version diffs.

For example, instead of saying:

> “Paper submitted December 2024, published June 2025, therefore pre-SAT.”

we can ask:

> “Its 2024 version contained A and B. SAT publicly disclosed C on Feb. 2, D on Mar. 5, and the C→D relationship on Apr. 2. The paper’s May revision first adds C+D.”

That would be genuinely probative.

We should also make the index **historically literal**. No importing later H(s)H interpretations into an older SAT episode. If an episode says “filament,” “timesheet,” “null,” “vacuum,” “dark photon,” “24-cell,” or some older formulation, we record exactly that formulation first and only add a separate normalized/conceptual mapping field afterward.

And because rejected material may still matter for diffusion, every proposition should retain its historical release status even if SAT later abandoned it. A 24-cell claim publicly released in 2025 stays in the exposure index forever as a 2025 exposure event.

I’d treat this as a prerequisite dataset with three confidence classes:

**A — transcript-backed exact disclosure date**  
**B — episode metadata/description establishes disclosure, transcript incomplete**  
**C — inferred from later references but public content not yet recovered**

The first pass should probably start with every clearly SAT-bearing episode from February 2025 onward and then expand outward to episodes that contain partial or precursor material. We already have anchors like Feb. 2, 2025; Jan. 16, 2026; Mar. 5, 2026; Apr. 2, 2026; and the Dec. 28 archive-release episode, but those should be treated as seed records, not the index itself.

This should become one of the central Cross tables, because it lets us convert vague chronology into a proper **public-information frontier** for every day in the investigation."
          ]

The isomorphism is a mathematical identity: the curvature patterns that define relativistic trajectories are directly related to the eigenvalue spectrum that defines quantum states.

	•	Worldlines $X(\lambda)$ are constrained to the hypersphere $S^3$ of radius $R$:

parts:
Yes. I’m reprioritizing the original `SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25` accordingly.

The important correction is that the 101-episode `HSH_RESOURCES/EXPOSURE_STATS/PODCAST_GUIDE` build should not be treated as the main surviving corpus with gaps around it. It’s better regarded as a partial derivative index. The original archive may still contain some of the largest podcast-era deposits, potentially in bulk transcript/conversation collections whose filenames or paths don’t contain obvious `PODCAST`/`DEBATING` labels—which would explain why the simple repository searches are missing material we know should exist.

So the search hierarchy is now:

1. **Original SAT archive first:** inventory its large directory clusters and identify podcast-heavy aggregations even when they aren’t explicitly named `PODCAST`.
2. Within those, recover the episode/date/title spine and identify bundled or duplicated transcript sets.
3. Then use the explicit `PODCAST` and `DEBATING` collections in all three repos as cross-checks and gap-fillers.
4. Finally reconcile against `PODCAST_GUIDE`, `PODCAST_EPs`, the `CROSS_TRANSCRIPT_*` material, and episode-ranking data.
5. Only after that coverage pass do we regard concept-first-occurrence results as reasonably mature.

I’m also broadening discovery beyond directory names. We should look for large deposits recognizable by **episode numbering, show-title variants, dates, recurring intro/outro language, transcript structure, and known episode titles**. Otherwise a big old podcast dump sitting under an archival or subject heading could remain invisible to a `PODCAST` string search.

And this matters beyond simply getting the episode count above 101. The original archive is likely where we have the best chance of recovering the **early 2025 public-development sequence**, which is precisely the high-value interval for statements like:

> concept X is publicly present by date Y

and eventually, with sufficient coverage:

> the earliest public occurrence we have located is episode N on date Y.

I’ll treat finding those large original-archive podcast reservoirs as the immediate top-of-rotation task.

If working in any of the repos, the first thing to do (and revisit frequently) is to read welcome/orientation/guidance/tools/wyafinding and other working documents. My Dashboard is also at your disposal.

Agreed. I’ll treat orientation as a mandatory preflight, not optional housekeeping: before substantive repo work, I’ll read the current welcome/orientation/guidance/tools/wayfinding materials, and I’ll re-check them periodically for workflow changes. I’ll also use your Dashboard as a coordination surface rather than relying on stale assumptions from prior turns.

This is the first theory read.\n\t2.\tFundamental Intuitions Extended (FIE) — the foundational conceptual/doctrinal source. The ancestry is FIE → SAT → H(s)H. 	1.	BEDROCK.md — the central living theory-premise control surface. This is the first theory read.
	2.	Fundamental Intuitions Extended (FIE) — the foundational conceptual/doctrinal source. The ancestry is FIE → SAT → H(s)H. For SAT it is essentially the core doctrine; for H(s)H, nearly so.

	8.	HSH_RESOURCES orientation — active supporting resources; not generally quarantined.
	9.	RESOURCES Toolkit orientation — primary supporting mathematics/resources repository.

	12.	LIBRARY.md

	17.	The relevant primary SAT/H(s)H source documents identified by BEDROCK/FIE for the particular problem being worked.

BEDROCK → FIE/primary source → STATE → current specialist state → sandbox work.

thoughts.content: I’m treating the original archive as the primary podcast reservoir and applying the mandatory orientation review before repository work. I’m prioritizing episode recovery, public-availability distinctions, transcript evidence, attribution, confidence, and unresolved gaps.

I’m consolidating episode metadata, provenance, transcript-confirmed concepts, attribution, historical variants, and evidence levels. The index should recover every available episode, identify missing records explicitly, and support both episode-first and concept-first timelines.

I’m preserving factual records, provenance, arguments, hypotheses, revisions, and unresolved conflicts as distinct layers. I’m also tracking supersession, historical definitions, terminology links, and cautious chronology without treating sequence as proof of influence.

thoughts.summary: Refreshed archive workflow, structured chronology, and separated evidence layers
